prereqs: Propositional logic: statements and truth values
lesson:
# What electronic design automation is

Electronic design automation (EDA) is the software that turns an idea for an electronic system into something a factory can build and a tester can check. It covers integrated circuits, printed circuit boards and packages. Older names overlap with it: ECAD (electronic computer-aided design) and CAE (computer-aided engineering). For a tool designer the key fact is that every EDA program is an algorithm over a precise model: a graph, a set of Boolean functions, a geometry database or a system of equations.

## Design, analysis and verification tools

EDA tools fall into three kinds by what they do to a design. Synthesis or implementation tools transform it: logic synthesis turns register-transfer code into gates, a placer assigns cells to locations, a router draws wires. Analysis tools compute a property without changing anything: a static timer computes arrival times and slack, an extractor computes resistance and capacitance, a power tool computes switching power. Verification tools check that two descriptions agree or that a property holds: a simulator runs test stimulus, an equivalence checker proves that a netlist matches its RTL, a design-rule checker proves that layout geometry obeys the foundry's rules. Most real tools mix the three: an optimizer calls an analyzer inside its loop.

## Every tool is an algorithm on a model

A tool never sees the chip. It sees a model. A gate netlist is a hypergraph whose vertices are cells and whose hyperedges are nets. A timing graph is a directed acyclic graph with delays on its edges. Logic is a Boolean network, often stored as an and-inverter graph. Layout is a set of polygons on numbered layers. Circuit simulation is a system of nonlinear differential-algebraic equations. Once the model is fixed, the tool's job is a classical problem: shortest paths, partitioning, satisfiability, sparse linear solves, computational geometry. That is why an applied mathematician can learn to write EDA tools.

## Why automation is unavoidable

A modern chip holds billions of transistors and is checked against thousands of geometric rules and many timing scenarios. No team can place, wire or check that by hand. Automation also makes design repeatable: the same inputs and settings give the same layout, so engineers can change one thing and measure its effect. The cost is that tool quality now bounds chip quality. A placer that wastes 5% of wirelength, or a timer that is pessimistic by 20 ps, costs power, area or frequency on every chip that uses it.

## Going deeper

Lavagno, Markov, Martin and Scheffer (eds.), "Electronic Design Automation for IC System Design, Verification, and Testing" and its companion volume on implementation (2nd ed., 2016).

problems.q:
Which of these is a verification tool rather than a transformation or analysis tool?

A) A static timer computing slack

B) An equivalence checker comparing RTL with its synthesized netlist

C) A router drawing wires on metal layers

D) A placer assigning cells to rows
problems.a: An equivalence checker comparing RTL with its synthesized netlist
problems.e: Verification checks that two descriptions agree or that a property holds; the equivalence checker proves the netlist matches the RTL.

problems.q:
A tool reads a routed layout and reports the resistance and capacitance of every net, without changing the layout. What kind of tool is it?

A) An analysis tool

B) A synthesis tool

C) A verification tool

D) An implementation tool
problems.a: An analysis tool
problems.e: It computes a property of the design and changes nothing, which is what an analysis tool does.

problems.q:
A gate-sizing optimizer upsizes cells on failing paths and re-times after every few moves. What does this illustrate?

A) An analysis tool that never changes the design

B) Two independent tools that never share data

C) An implementation tool calling an analysis engine inside its loop

D) A verification tool proving functional correctness
problems.a: An implementation tool calling an analysis engine inside its loop
problems.e: Optimizers transform the design but need an analyzer, here a timer, to score each change.

problems.q:
A circuit simulator such as SPICE turns a transistor netlist into what kind of mathematical problem?

A) A shortest-path problem on a DAG

B) A rectangle-packing problem

C) A system of nonlinear differential-algebraic equations

D) A Boolean satisfiability instance
problems.a: A system of nonlinear differential-algebraic equations
problems.e: Kirchhoff's laws plus nonlinear device equations and capacitor dynamics give a DAE system solved by Newton iteration and implicit integration.

A) A truth table of the whole design

B) A polygon database on numbered layers

C) A hypergraph whose hyperedges are nets

D) A matrix of node voltages
problems.a: A hypergraph whose hyperedges are nets
problems.e: A net can connect many cells, so the natural model is a hypergraph, and the cut counts hyperedges that span both sides.

problems.a: A hypergraph whose hyperedges are nets

Which statement best describes the relationship between EDA and the older terms ECAD and CAE?

A) CAE refers only to manufacturing equipment

B) They overlap: all name software that designs and analyzes electronics

C) They are unrelated fields with separate tools

D) ECAD is only for mechanical parts
problems.a: They overlap: all name software that designs and analyzes electronics

problems.q:
Why can no design team place and route a modern chip by hand?

A) Billions of devices and thousands of rules exceed any manual effort

B) Hand-drawn wires cannot be manufactured

C) Computers draw thinner wires than people can

D) Manual layout is forbidden by foundry contracts
problems.a: Billions of devices and thousands of rules exceed any manual effort
problems.e: Scale is the reason: the number of objects and checks is far beyond manual work.

problems.q:
A placer systematically produces 5% more wirelength than a competitor's on the same designs. What does this cost the chip?

A) Only the size of the DEF file

B) Nothing, because routing fixes wirelength

C) Delay, power and routability on every design that uses it

D) Only simulation run time
problems.a: Delay, power and routability on every design that uses it
problems.e: Tool quality bounds chip quality: longer wires add capacitance, delay and power and make routing harder.

# Integrated circuits and VLSI scale

An integrated circuit puts transistors and their wiring on one piece of silicon. The names SSI, MSI, LSI, VLSI and ULSI (small, medium, large, very large and ultra large scale integration) count how many devices fit on a chip, and today's chips hold billions. Scale is the reason EDA exists: every tool must run in time roughly linear, or $n \log n$, in the size of the design, because anything quadratic is already too slow.

## Integration levels and exponential growth

The integration names grew from tens of gates (SSI) to thousands (LSI) to hundreds of thousands and beyond (VLSI). The cut-off numbers vary by author, so treat them as orders of magnitude, not definitions. Behind the growth is the observation usually called Moore's law: the number of transistors on a chip of given cost doubled roughly every two years for decades. If a chip holds $N_0$ transistors and the count doubles every $T$ years, then after $y$ years it holds $N_0 \cdot 2^{y/T}$. Starting from 2 billion with $T = 2$, eight years later the count is $2 \cdot 2^4 = 32$ billion.

## Why exhaustive methods fail

A block with $n$ input bits has $2^n$ input combinations. At 40 inputs that is $2^{40} \approx 1.1 \times 10^{12}$ vectors. A simulator that evaluates $10^9$ vectors per second needs about 1100 seconds. At 64 inputs the same simulator needs about 585 years. So EDA cannot enumerate. It uses structure instead: symbolic representations that share work (BDDs and AIGs), solvers that prune (SAT), and analyses that avoid enumerating input patterns altogether (static timing analysis computes worst cases over a graph rather than simulating vectors). The same blow-up applies to state: a design with 100 flip-flops has $2^{100}$ possible states.

## The design productivity gap

Transistor counts grew faster than the number of engineers. Suppose a skilled layout engineer draws 100 transistors per working day and a year has 250 working days. A 10-million-transistor design then needs $10^7 / (100 \cdot 250) = 400$ engineer-years of drawing alone, before any checking. Modern chips are hundreds of times larger. The gap between what the process can build and what a team can design by hand is closed only by raising the abstraction level (writing RTL instead of drawing transistors) and by reusing blocks. Every concept in this curriculum is a piece of that closing.

## Going deeper

Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits: A Design Perspective" (2nd ed., 2003), chapter 1.

problems.q: A chip family holds 5 billion transistors today. If the count doubles every 3 years, how many billion transistors will a chip of the same cost hold after 9 years?
problems.e: 9 years is 3 doubling periods, so the count is $5 \cdot 2^{3} = 40$ billion.

problems.q: A chip family holds 3 billion transistors today. If the count doubles every 2 years, how many billion transistors will a chip of the same cost hold after 8 years?
problems.e: 8 years is 4 doubling periods, so the count is $3 \cdot 2^{4} = 48$ billion.

problems.e: 12 years is 4 doubling periods, so the count is $2 \cdot 2^{4} = 32$ billion.

problems.e: There are $2^{42}$ vectors. Dividing by $10^{10}$ per second and by 3600 seconds per hour gives 0.12 hours.

problems.e: There are $2^{45}$ vectors. Dividing by $10^{8}$ per second and by 3600 seconds per hour gives 97.73 hours.

problems.e: There are $2^{50}$ vectors. Dividing by $10^{9}$ per second and by 3600 seconds per hour gives 312.75 hours.

problems.e: $20 \times 10^6 / (150 \cdot 220) = 606.1$ engineer-years, before any checking or rework.

problems.q: An engineer drawing layout by hand completes 100 transistors per working day, and a year has 250 working days. How many engineer-years would it take to draw a design of 2 million transistors? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: $2 \times 10^6 / (100 \cdot 250) = 80$ engineer-years, before any checking or rework.

label: Abstraction levels from system to layout
lesson:
# Abstraction levels from system to layout

Designers describe a chip at several levels of abstraction: system, algorithm or behavior, register transfer, gate, transistor and layout. Each level hides detail that the level below fills in. EDA tools are mostly translators and checkers between adjacent levels, so knowing what each level keeps and drops tells you what a tool can compute from it and what it must assume.

## The ladder of levels

At the system level a design is a set of communicating components (processors, memories, accelerators, interconnect) with throughput and latency budgets. At the behavioral level it is an algorithm, often in C++ or SystemC, with no clock. At the register-transfer level (RTL) it is registers and the combinational logic between them, cycle by cycle, written in Verilog, SystemVerilog or VHDL. At the gate level it is a netlist of library cells such as NAND2 and DFF. At the transistor level it is a circuit of MOSFETs, resistors and capacitors. At the layout level it is polygons on mask layers. Gajski and Kuhn's Y-chart organizes the same idea along three views (behavioral, structural, physical) with these levels as rings.

## What each level keeps and drops

Going down the ladder adds information. RTL fixes the cycle on which each value is computed but not which gates compute it. The gate netlist fixes the gates but not where they sit. Layout fixes geometry, and with it the wire resistance and capacitance that set real delay. Going up hides information, which is what makes large designs tractable: RTL simulation runs much faster than transistor simulation because it ignores voltages and computes one value per signal per cycle. The price is that a property that depends on dropped detail (exact delay, crosstalk, IR drop) cannot be computed at the higher level, only estimated.

## Refinement and checking between levels

Every step down is a refinement, and every refinement can introduce an error. So the flow pairs each transformation with a check that the levels agree. Logic synthesis is checked by logic equivalence checking between RTL and netlist. Layout is checked by layout-versus-schematic (LVS), which extracts a transistor netlist from polygons and compares it with the intended one. Timing estimated at a high level is re-checked once real parasitics are known. When a check fails, the designer goes back up a level. This is the first reason flows iterate. Each check is itself an EDA engine, so the checks scale with the design just as the transformations do.

## Going deeper

Gajski and Kuhn, "Guest Editors' Introduction: New VLSI Tools", IEEE Computer (1983), which introduced the Y-chart.

problems.q:
Which is a register-transfer-level description?

A) Polygons on the metal-1 layer

B) A block diagram of processors and memories

C) Verilog that says what each register holds after every clock edge

D) A list of MOSFETs with widths and lengths
problems.a: Verilog that says what each register holds after every clock edge
problems.e: RTL describes registers and the combinational logic between them, cycle by cycle.

problems.q:
On the Gajski-Kuhn Y-chart, a floorplan of blocks on a die belongs to which view?

A) The temporal view

B) The physical view

C) The behavioral view

D) The structural view
problems.a: The physical view
problems.e: The Y-chart has behavioral, structural and physical axes; floorplans and layouts are physical.

problems.q:
A C++ model computes a video filter with no notion of clock cycles. At which level is it?

A) Gate level

B) Register-transfer level

C) Behavioral or algorithmic level

D) System floorplan level
problems.a: Behavioral or algorithmic level
problems.e: An untimed algorithm is a behavioral description; RTL fixes cycle-by-cycle register behaviour.

problems.q:
Going from RTL to a gate netlist adds which information?

A) The polygons on each mask layer

B) The cycle on which each value is computed

C) Which library cells implement the logic

D) Where each cell sits on the die
problems.a: Which library cells implement the logic
problems.e: RTL already fixes cycles; synthesis chooses the gates. Placement and layout add positions and geometry later.

problems.q:
A designer estimates crosstalk delay from RTL. Why is the estimate unreliable?

A) RTL simulators cannot run long tests

B) Crosstalk depends on neighbouring routed wires that RTL does not contain

C) Crosstalk is a purely logical effect

D) RTL contains too much geometric detail
problems.a: Crosstalk depends on neighbouring routed wires that RTL does not contain
problems.e: Crosstalk needs coupling capacitance between real wires, which exists only after routing.

problems.q:
Which quantity cannot be computed exactly from a gate-level netlist alone?

A) Wire delay set by routed resistance and capacitance

B) The fanout of each net

C) The number of cell instances

D) The logic function of the design
problems.a: Wire delay set by routed resistance and capacitance
problems.e: The netlist has no geometry; wire delay needs placement, routing and extraction.

problems.q:
Which check guards the step from transistor netlist to layout polygons?

A) Logic equivalence checking

B) Static timing analysis

C) Code coverage

D) Layout versus schematic (LVS)
problems.a: Layout versus schematic (LVS)
problems.e: LVS extracts devices and connections from the polygons and compares them with the intended netlist.

problems.q:
Which check guards the step from transistor netlist to layout polygons?

A) Logic equivalence checking

B) Static timing analysis

C) Layout versus schematic (LVS)

D) Code coverage
problems.a: Layout versus schematic (LVS)
problems.e: LVS extracts devices and connections from the polygons and compares them with the intended netlist.

problems.q:
Which check guards the step from RTL to a synthesized gate netlist?

A) Logic equivalence checking

B) Electromigration analysis

C) Layout versus schematic

D) Design-rule checking
problems.a: Logic equivalence checking
problems.e: Equivalence checking proves that the netlist computes the same function as the RTL.

lesson:
# Hierarchy, top-down and bottom-up design

A chip is never designed as one flat list of billions of cells. It is a tree of modules: the top instantiates subsystems, which instantiate blocks, which instantiate library cells. Hierarchy lets a team divide the work, lets a tool analyze a block once and reuse the result, and is the structure that top-down planning and bottom-up assembly operate on. Its cost is that optimization across a boundary becomes harder.

## Definitions, instances and flattening

A module definition is written once. An instance is one use of it. The instantiation structure is a rooted tree (more exactly a DAG of definitions, unrolled into a tree of instances). Flattening replaces every instance by a copy of its contents until only leaf cells remain. To count the flattened cells, multiply along each root-to-leaf path. If the top holds 4 instances of block A and 3 of block B, A holds 10 cells of its own plus 2 instances of C, C holds 25 cells and B holds 40 cells, then the flattened design has $4(10 + 2 \cdot 25) + 3 \cdot 40 = 360$ cells.

## Top-down and bottom-up

In top-down design the architect splits the system into blocks, gives each block a budget (area, timing at its ports, power) and refines each block independently. In bottom-up design, proven blocks (cells, memories, IP cores) are built and characterized first and then assembled. Real projects do both: the floorplan and budgets come top-down, while library cells, memories and hard IP come bottom-up. The meeting point is the block boundary, where top-down budgets must match bottom-up characterizations. A budget that the block cannot meet sends the plan back up the tree.

## What hierarchy buys and costs

A hierarchical tool stores and analyzes each definition once. In the example, the definitions hold $10 + 25 + 40 = 75$ cells against 360 flattened, almost five times fewer. Timing tools use extracted block models (interface logic models, extracted timing models) for the same reason. The cost is lost optimization: a synthesizer that keeps boundaries cannot merge logic across them, and a placer that keeps a block in a fixed region cannot interleave it with its neighbours. Flows therefore flatten selectively: small blocks are flattened for quality, large ones kept hierarchical for capacity and team ownership.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective" (4th ed., 2010), chapter 1 on hierarchy, regularity, modularity and locality.

problems.q: The top module instantiates 3 copies of block A and 5 copies of block B. Block A contains 10 standard cells of its own plus 2 instances of block C. Block C contains 22 standard cells. Block B contains 27 standard cells. How many standard cells does the fully flattened design contain?
problems.e: Multiply along each path from the top: $3(10 + 2 \cdot 22) + 5 \cdot 27 = 297$ cells.

Block B contains 73 standard cells. Counting only block instances (A, B and C, not standard cells), how many block instances does the flattened design contain?

Block B contains 42 standard cells. Counting only block instances (A, B and C, not standard cells), how many block instances does the flattened design contain?
problems.e: There are 6 A instances and 3 B instances, and each A holds 1 C instances, so $6 + 3 + 6 \cdot 1 = 15$.

Block B contains 43 standard cells. Counting only block instances (A, B and C, not standard cells), how many block instances does the flattened design contain?
problems.e: There are 2 A instances and 2 B instances, and each A holds 1 C instances, so $2 + 2 + 2 \cdot 1 = 6$.

Block B contains 60 standard cells. A hierarchical tool stores each block definition once. How many times more standard cells does the flattened design hold than the definitions of A, B and C together? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Flattened: 364 cells. Definitions: $12 + 60 + 32 = 104$ cells. Ratio: 3.5.

Block B contains 49 standard cells. A hierarchical tool stores each block definition once. How many times more standard cells does the flattened design hold than the definitions of A, B and C together? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Flattened: 257 cells. Definitions: $13 + 49 + 40 = 102$ cells. Ratio: 2.52.

Block B contains 76 standard cells. A hierarchical tool stores each block definition once. lesson:
# ASICs, FPGAs and systems on chip

Three product kinds dominate digital hardware. An application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) is fabricated for one purpose. A field-programmable gate array (FPGA) is a fixed chip whose logic and wiring are configured after manufacture. A system on chip (SoC) integrates processors, memories, accelerators and interfaces on one die, and may be built as an ASIC or prototyped on an FPGA. Their economics decide which flow a team runs.

## Three ways to build digital logic

An ASIC is designed down to masks: the team owns every transistor's placement and pays for a mask set and fabrication. It gives the best power, performance and area, but mistakes are fixed only by a new mask set. An FPGA is an array of lookup tables, flip-flops, memories and DSP blocks with programmable routing. Its flow ends in a bitstream, not masks, so a bug fix is a reconfiguration. The programmability costs area, speed and power relative to an ASIC of the same function. An SoC is an architecture, not a fabric: it names what is integrated (CPU cores, caches, a network on chip, peripherals), and it is usually an ASIC built largely from IP blocks.

## Non-recurring and unit cost

The choice between ASIC and FPGA is a cost model. An ASIC has a large non-recurring engineering cost $F_A$ (design, verification, masks) and a small unit cost $u_A$. An FPGA has a small non-recurring cost $F_F$ and a larger unit cost $u_F$. Total costs are equal at the break-even volume
$$N^* = \frac{F_A - F_F}{u_F - u_A}.$$
With $F_A = 5{,}000{,}000$, $F_F = 200{,}000$, $u_A = 4$ and $u_F = 64$ (all in dollars), $N^* = 4{,}800{,}000 / 60 = 80{,}000$ units. Above that volume the ASIC is cheaper. Below that volume the FPGA wins.

## Choosing and combining

Volume is not the only input. Time to market favours FPGAs, since there is no fabrication wait. Power or performance limits favour ASICs. Standards that are still changing favour reprogrammability. Many teams do both: they prototype and emulate an SoC on FPGAs to run software early, then tape out the ASIC. Some products embed programmable logic inside an ASIC, or pair a processor SoC with FPGA fabric on one die. For an EDA engineer the consequence is two families of back-end tools: placement and routing onto a fixed FPGA fabric, and full-custom placement and routing onto silicon.

## Going deeper

Kuon and Rose, "Measuring the Gap Between FPGAs and ASICs", IEEE Transactions on CAD (2007).

problems.q:
What does an ASIC team pay for that an FPGA team does not?

A) Synthesis of RTL into logic

B) Static timing analysis

C) A mask set and wafer fabrication for its own design

D) Functional verification
problems.a: A mask set and wafer fabrication for its own design
problems.e: Both teams synthesize, time and verify; only the ASIC team fabricates its own masks.

problems.q:
Relative to an ASIC of the same function, an FPGA implementation typically has what?

A) Identical area but higher speed

B) Less area, higher speed and lower power

C) More area, lower speed and higher power

D) Lower unit cost at every volume
problems.a: More area, lower speed and higher power
problems.e: Programmable lookup tables and routing switches cost area, delay and power compared with fixed logic.

Which blocks are found in a typical modern FPGA fabric?

A) Lookup tables, flip-flops, block RAMs and DSP blocks

B) Only NAND gates and inverters

C) Custom transistors drawn per design

D) Analog amplifiers configured by masks
problems.a: Lookup tables, flip-flops, block RAMs and DSP blocks
problems.e: FPGA fabrics combine LUT logic with hard memory and arithmetic blocks and programmable routing.

A) 172,413 units

B) 235,000 units

C) 470,000 units

D) 250,000 units

E) 162,068 units
problems.a: 235,000 units

problems.q:
An ASIC costs 4,000,000 dollars of non-recurring engineering and 11 dollars per unit. An FPGA solution costs 200,000 dollars of non-recurring engineering and 51 dollars per unit. At what volume do the two have equal total cost?

A) 100,000 units

B) 78,431 units

C) 95,000 units

D) 74,509 units

E) 190,000 units
problems.a: 95,000 units

problems.q:
An ASIC costs 3,000,000 dollars of non-recurring engineering and 10 dollars per unit. An FPGA solution costs 400,000 dollars of non-recurring engineering and 60 dollars per unit. At what volume do the two have equal total cost?

A) 52,000 units

B) 104,000 units

C) 60,000 units

D) 43,333 units

E) 50,000 units
problems.a: 52,000 units

problems.q:
Why do SoC teams often run their design on FPGAs before tape-out?

A) To generate the mask layout

B) To replace the need for an ASIC

C) To measure ASIC leakage power exactly

D) To run real software on the hardware early, at near-real speed
problems.a: To run real software on the hardware early, at near-real speed
problems.e: FPGA prototyping and emulation run far faster than simulation, so software and hardware can be validated together.

problems.q:
Why does the ASIC-versus-FPGA choice give rise to two families of back-end tools?

A) ASIC tools cannot read RTL

B) One maps onto a fixed programmable fabric, the other places and routes onto custom silicon

C) The two use incompatible HDLs

D) FPGA tools need no placement at all
problems.a: One maps onto a fixed programmable fabric, the other places and routes onto custom silicon
problems.e: FPGA implementation selects among existing sites and wires; ASIC implementation creates the layout itself.

problems.q:
A product's protocol standard is still changing and it must ship in four months. Which choice fits?

A) Neither; the standard must be frozen first

B) An ASIC, because masks can be changed in the field

C) An FPGA, for time to market and reprogrammability

D) A full-custom ASIC, for lowest unit cost
problems.a: An FPGA, for time to market and reprogrammability
problems.e: FPGAs avoid fabrication delays and can be updated as the standard changes.

# IP cores and standard-cell libraries as products

Almost nothing on a modern chip is designed from scratch. Standard cells, memories, I/O cells, PHYs and processor cores are bought or reused as intellectual-property (IP) products. A design team assembles them, and EDA tools consume the views each product ships with. A tool designer must know what those views are, because every engine reads them.

## Soft, firm and hard IP

Soft IP is delivered as synthesizable RTL: a processor core, a bus fabric, a controller. It is portable across processes but must be synthesized, placed and timed by the buyer. Hard IP is delivered as finished layout for one specific process: a SerDes PHY, a PLL, an SRAM macro, an analog block. It has proven timing and power but cannot be moved to another process without redesign. Firm IP sits between, for example a gate netlist with placement guidance. The more physical the delivery, the less freedom the integrator has and the less risk they carry.

## The standard-cell library

A standard-cell library is a set of small logic cells (inverters, NANDs, multiplexers, flip-flops, often several drive strengths and threshold-voltage flavours each) drawn to a common height so they abut in rows with shared power rails. It is a product with many views: Liberty files give timing, power and function per corner; LEF gives the cell outline, pin shapes and blockages for placement and routing; GDSII gives the full layout; SPICE netlists give the transistor circuit for LVS and characterization; Verilog models give simulation behaviour. A missing or inconsistent view breaks a specific stage: a Liberty file without a corner means that corner cannot be timed.

## Characterization and reuse economics

Library and IP vendors characterize each cell by running thousands of circuit simulations across input slew, output load, voltage and temperature, and tabulating the results into Liberty. That work is paid back by reuse: one library serves every design on the process. The same logic drives IP licensing: a team pays a licence fee and often a royalty per unit because designing and verifying a PCIe PHY or a CPU core itself would cost more and take longer. The integration risk moves to the interfaces, so IP ships with integration guides, constraints and verification models.

## Going deeper

Chinnery and Keutzer, "Closing the Gap Between ASIC and Custom" (2002), on how library quality limits ASIC performance.

# Hardware-software co-design

A system's function can run in software on a processor or in dedicated hardware. Hardware-software co-design decides that split together with the architecture, instead of building the hardware first and fitting software on afterwards. The decision is quantitative: how much of the runtime moves to hardware, how fast that hardware is, and what it costs in area and power. Amdahl's law is the first computation every architect runs.

## Partitioning a function

Profile the software and find the kernels that dominate runtime: a filter, a matrix multiply, a cryptographic round. Each kernel is a candidate for an accelerator. Moving it to hardware gains speed and energy but costs area, design effort and flexibility, and adds communication between processor and accelerator. Co-design tools and methods (system-level models in SystemC, high-level synthesis from C++, virtual platforms that run real software on a model of the hardware) let both sides be evaluated before RTL is frozen. Getting the split wrong is expensive: an accelerator for a kernel that turns out to be 5% of runtime is wasted silicon.

## Amdahl's law

If a fraction $f$ of the original runtime is accelerated by a factor $s$ and the rest is unchanged, the overall speedup is
$$S = \frac{1}{(1 - f) + f/s}.$$
With $f = 0.8$ and $s = 10$, $S = 1/(0.2 + 0.08) = 3.57$. A program that took 100 ms now takes 28 ms. The bound as $s \to \infty$ is $1/(1 - f) = 5$: no accelerator, however fast, beats the part that stays in software. In the example, 80% acceleration bounds the speedup at 5 no matter how much hardware is spent.

## Sizing the accelerator

Invert the law to size the hardware. To reach an overall speedup $S$ with fraction $f$ accelerated, the accelerator needs
$$s = \frac{f}{1/S - (1 - f)},$$
which exists only when $S < 1/(1 - f)$. For $f = 0.8$ and a target of $S = 4$, $s = 0.8/(0.25 - 0.2) = 16$. Raising the target to 4.5 needs $s = 0.8/(0.2222 - 0.2) = 36$. Near the bound, each extra bit of speedup costs a much faster accelerator, which is a strong argument for accelerating more of the program rather than accelerating one kernel harder.

## Going deeper

De Micheli and Gupta, "Hardware/Software Co-Design", Proceedings of the IEEE (1997); Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach", chapter 1 on Amdahl's law.

# The RTL-to-GDSII flow end to end

The RTL-to-GDSII flow is the chain of tools that turns register-transfer code into the mask layout a foundry manufactures. It is the backbone of digital chip design and of this curriculum: almost every later domain is one stage of it, studied in depth. Knowing the order of the stages, and what each one hands the next, is how a tool designer knows what their engine can assume about its input.

## The stages in order

A digital flow runs: specification and architecture, RTL design, functional verification, logic synthesis, design-for-test (scan) insertion, floorplanning, placement, clock tree synthesis, routing, parasitic extraction, signoff (static timing, power and IR drop, design-rule and layout-versus-schematic checks), tape-out, then fabrication, packaging and production test. Verification is not a single box: it runs alongside RTL design and continues on the netlist. The front end is everything up to a verified netlist; the back end, or physical design, is floorplanning through signoff. Real flows add steps such as power-intent checks, timing-driven optimization after each physical stage, and engineering change orders late in signoff.

## What each stage hands the next

Each stage consumes one representation and produces a more detailed one. Synthesis reads RTL, constraints (SDC) and the Liberty library, and writes a gate netlist. Floorplanning adds a die outline, macro positions and the power grid. Placement adds a legal location for every standard cell. Clock tree synthesis adds buffers and wires that deliver the clock to every flip-flop with controlled skew. Routing adds the geometry of every wire and via. Extraction turns that geometry into resistances and capacitances (SPEF). Signoff reads all of it and either passes the design or reports violations. The final layout is streamed out as GDSII or OASIS.

## What becomes known at each stage

The flow is also a schedule of when information appears. Gate count and logic depth are first known after synthesis. Cell positions first exist after placement, so wirelength before placement is only an estimate. Clock skew is first real after clock tree synthesis. Wire geometry and coupling capacitance first exist after routing and extraction. Every earlier stage must therefore optimize against estimates of quantities that a later stage will compute exactly. When the estimate was wrong, a later stage fails and the flow loops back, which is the theme of design closure.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 1; the OpenROAD flow scripts, which implement the whole chain with open-source tools.

lesson:
# Specification, architecture and RTL

The front of the flow decides what the chip is before any tool decides how to build it. A specification states function, interfaces and targets; an architecture chooses the blocks, the memory system and the pipelines that meet those targets; RTL writes each block as registers and the logic between them. Decisions made here bound everything downstream, and no back-end tool can recover performance that the architecture did not leave room for.

## The specification

A specification fixes the function (instruction set, protocol, algorithm), the interfaces (bus standards, pins, clocks), and the targets: clock frequency, throughput, latency, power budget, area or cost, and reliability requirements. It is the reference that verification checks against, so ambiguity here becomes bugs later. Good specifications are partly executable: a reference model in C++ or Python that produces the expected outputs, from which tests and later formal properties are derived. Targets need margins and priorities: when frequency and power conflict later, the specification should say which one wins. Reliability, safety and security requirements, such as error-correcting memories or a secure boot path, also start here.

## Architecture: blocks, pipelines and budgets

The architect picks the micro-architecture: how many pipeline stages, which memories and how wide, which functions get dedicated hardware, which clock domains exist. Each choice trades power, performance and area. Adding a pipeline stage shortens the logic between registers so the clock can be faster, at the cost of latency, registers and power. The architect also writes budgets: each block gets an area, a power share and timing at its ports. These budgets are what floorplanning and timing closure later try to honour. Architects evaluate these choices with performance models long before RTL exists.

## RTL as the hand-off

RTL in Verilog, SystemVerilog or VHDL describes behaviour per clock cycle: what each register holds after the edge, as a function of inputs and current state. It is precise about cycles and silent about gates. Writing RTL is design, not transcription: the coding style decides whether synthesis infers a multiplexer or a priority chain, whether a memory becomes an SRAM macro or flip-flops, and whether the logic between two registers is short enough to meet the clock. Lint and clock-domain-crossing checks run on RTL before synthesis, because a structural problem found here costs minutes; found after layout it costs weeks.

## Going deeper

Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach" (6th ed., 2017); Harris and Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture".

lesson:
# Functional verification in the flow

Functional verification asks whether the design does what the specification says. It runs from the first RTL to the final netlist and consumes most of a chip project's engineering effort. Because exhaustive testing is impossible, verification is a measurement problem: generate stimulus, check results against a reference, and measure how much of the behaviour has been exercised. A tool designer meets it in simulators, formal engines and coverage databases.

## Simulation, formal and emulation

Simulation drives the RTL with test stimulus and compares outputs to a reference model. Constrained-random testbenches (for example with the UVM methodology) generate many legal stimuli automatically. Formal verification proves a property for all inputs, using SAT, BDD or model-checking engines, but scales only to bounded problems or blocks. Emulation and FPGA prototyping map the design onto special hardware and run it millions of times faster than software simulation, so real software can boot. Equivalence checking is a separate formal step: it proves two versions of the design, for example RTL and the synthesized netlist, compute the same function.

## Coverage closes the loop

Since tests cannot be exhaustive, teams measure coverage. Code coverage counts which lines, branches and toggles were exercised. Functional coverage counts which specified situations occurred, as bins: for a packet size field with 8 bins and a packet type with 4 bins, the cross coverage has $8 \cdot 4 = 32$ bins. If tests have hit 26 of them, functional coverage is $26/32 = 81.25\%$. Coverage holes direct the next tests. Full coverage does not prove correctness, only that every listed situation was seen at least once; the list itself can be incomplete.

## Why late bugs cost more

A bug found in RTL is fixed by editing code and re-running tests. Found after synthesis, it may need an engineering change order on the netlist and a new round of equivalence checking. Found after layout, it reopens placement and routing. Found in silicon, it needs a respin. A common rule of thumb models each later stage as multiplying the fix cost by about ten. Under that assumption a bug that costs 2 engineer-days in RTL costs about $2 \cdot 10^3 = 2000$ engineer-days if it escapes three stages to silicon. That multiplier, more than any other fact, explains verification's share of effort.

## Going deeper

Wile, Goss and Roesner, "Comprehensive Functional Verification: The Complete Industry Cycle" (2005); the Accellera UVM user guide.

label: Logic synthesis
prereqs: Logical equivalence, De Morgan and normal forms
lesson:
# Logic synthesis

Logic synthesis translates RTL into a netlist of cells from a target library, optimizing for timing, area and power under the constraints in an SDC file. It is the first stage where the design meets the technology, and the first where timing can be computed from real cell delays. Tools include Synopsys Design Compiler and Cadence Genus commercially, and Yosys with ABC in open source.

## Elaboration and generic logic

Synthesis first elaborates the RTL: it resolves parameters and hierarchy, infers registers from clocked processes, infers multiplexers from conditional assignments, and recognizes arithmetic operators and memories. The result is a technology-independent Boolean network: registers plus combinational logic expressed as generic gates or as an and-inverter graph. No library cell has been chosen yet. Inference rules matter: an incompletely specified combinational assignment infers a latch, which is a frequent and costly surprise. Elaboration also flattens or preserves hierarchy as directed, resolves generate loops, and records which RTL signals became which registers, information that equivalence checking and debugging rely on later.

## Optimization and technology mapping

Technology-independent optimization restructures the Boolean network to reduce its size and depth: it removes redundancy, shares common subexpressions and rebalances logic, while preserving the function. Technology mapping then covers the network with cells from the Liberty library, choosing for each region the cell (or cells) that implement it at the lowest cost: area under a delay constraint, or delay under an area budget. After mapping, the tool sizes gates, inserts buffers and may restructure critical paths, using static timing analysis on the mapped netlist as its guide. Mapping quality depends directly on the library: more cell functions and drive strengths give the mapper more options.

## Correctness and what synthesis cannot see

Synthesis must preserve the function, and logic equivalence checking proves that it did, by matching registers between RTL and netlist and checking that each register's next-state logic is equivalent. Synthesis also works with limited physical information. Classic flows estimate wire delay from fanout with a wire-load model, which can be badly wrong in deep-submicron processes where wires dominate delay. Physically aware synthesis runs a quick placement to estimate wirelength instead. A netlist that met timing in synthesis but fails after placement is the classic symptom of that gap. Both effects show why synthesis and placement are increasingly run as one optimization.

## Going deeper

De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994); Hachtel and Somenzi, "Logic Synthesis and Verification Algorithms" (1996); the Yosys and ABC documentation.

lesson:
# Design for test and scan insertion

A fabricated chip can have manufacturing defects that no design review could find, so each die is tested before it ships. Design for test (DFT) adds hardware that makes testing possible in seconds: scan chains, test compression, built-in self-test for memories and boundary scan for board-level tests. Scan insertion runs during or right after synthesis, and it changes the netlist that every later stage sees.

## Scan chains

A sequential circuit is hard to test because its internal state is hard to set and observe. Scan replaces each flip-flop with a scan flip-flop that has a multiplexer at its input. In test mode the flops are connected into shift registers, called scan chains. The tester shifts a pattern into the chains, pulses the functional clock once to capture the combinational logic's response, and shifts the result out. The sequential test problem becomes a combinational one, which automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) can solve. With $F$ scan flops split as evenly as possible into $C$ chains, the longest chain has $L = \lceil F/C \rceil$ flops.

## Test time

Test time is dominated by shifting. With $N$ patterns and chain length $L$, the first pattern is shifted in over $L$ cycles; then each pattern takes one capture cycle followed by $L$ cycles that shift its response out while the next pattern shifts in. The total is $(N + 1)L + N$ cycles. For $F = 20{,}000$ flops in $C = 16$ chains, $L = 1250$. With $N = 2000$ patterns, the test takes $2001 \cdot 1250 + 2000 = 2{,}503{,}250$ cycles, which at a 50 MHz shift clock is about 50.07 ms.

## What DFT costs the rest of the flow

Every scan flop is slightly larger and slower than a plain flop, and the scan connections add wires. Placement reorders the scan chains to follow cell locations, since a chain stitched in netlist order would zig-zag across the die. More chains shorten test time but need more tester pins, which is why compression logic expands a few external channels into many internal chains. Testers are expensive per second, so test time is product cost. DFT is therefore a flow-wide trade: area and timing on one side, test cost and defect coverage on the other.

## Going deeper

Bushnell and Agrawal, "Essentials of Electronic Testing for Digital, Memory and Mixed-Signal VLSI Circuits" (2000), chapters on scan design.

lesson:
# Floorplanning and power planning

Floorplanning is the first physical step. It chooses the die and core size, places the large blocks (memories, analog macros, hard IP), arranges the I/O, and lays down the power distribution network. Every later physical stage works inside the floorplan, so a bad floorplan, such as a memory in the wrong corner or a starved power grid, cannot be fixed by a better placer or router.

## Core area from utilization

The core is the region that holds standard cells and macros, inside the I/O ring. Its size starts from the cell area reported by synthesis and a target utilization, the fraction of core area occupied by cells. Placement and routing need white space for buffers, wires and later fixes, so typical targets are well below 100%. If the cells and macros cover $A_{cell} = 1{,}200{,}000\ \mu m^2$ and the target utilization is $u = 0.7$, the core area is $A_{core} = A_{cell}/u \approx 1{,}714{,}286\ \mu m^2$. Choosing too high a utilization saves area but makes routing and timing closure fail later.

## Shape, rows and the die

With an aspect ratio $r = H/W$, the core width is $W = \sqrt{A_{core}/r}$ and height $H = rW$. For a square core in the example, $W = H \approx 1309.3\ \mu m$. The core is divided into standard-cell rows whose height equals the library's cell height. The die adds a margin for the I/O ring and seal: with a margin $m$ on each side, the die is $(W + 2m)(H + 2m)$. With $m = 100\ \mu m$ the die is about $1509.3 \times 1509.3\ \mu m$, or about $2.278\ mm^2$.

## Macros and the power grid

Macros are placed before standard cells. Good practice puts them near the edges, leaves channels between them for routing, and orients their pins toward the logic they talk to. A poor macro placement creates long wires and routing congestion that no later stage can fix. Power planning builds the grid: power rings around the core, straps on upper metal layers, and rails along each row. The grid must keep the voltage drop (IR drop) at every cell within budget while consuming as little routing resource as possible, so its density is a trade between signal routability and supply integrity.

## Going deeper

label: Placement
lesson:
# Placement

Placement assigns every standard cell a legal location in the rows of the floorplan. Its objective is short wires, because wirelength drives delay, power and routability, subject to density limits and timing. Modern placers are analytical: they solve a smooth optimization for approximate positions, then legalize them into rows and sites and refine locally. OpenROAD's global placer and the RePlAce algorithm are open-source examples.

## Half-perimeter wirelength

A placer cannot route every candidate placement, so it estimates each net's wire with the half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL): the half-perimeter of the smallest axis-aligned box that contains all its pins,
$$\mathrm{HPWL} = (x_{max} - x_{min}) + (y_{max} - y_{min}).$$
For pins at $(2, 3)$, $(7, 1)$ and $(4, 6)$ the box spans $x$ from 2 to 7 and $y$ from 1 to 6, so HPWL $= 5 + 5 = 10$. For two- and three-pin nets HPWL equals the shortest rectilinear Steiner tree length; for larger nets it is a lower bound. It is cheap and is the standard placement objective.

## Total wirelength and incremental moves

The placer's objective sums HPWL over all nets, often with timing-critical nets weighted higher. Because a cell touches only its own nets, moving one cell changes only those nets' terms. A placer evaluating a move recomputes HPWL for just the affected nets and takes the difference, which is how detailed placement can try millions of swaps cheaply. If a move shrinks one net's box by 4 and stretches another's by 1, the total improves by 3. The same locality makes HPWL easy to update incrementally inside an analytical placer, where the smooth approximations of HPWL are differentiated with respect to each cell's coordinates.

## Density, legality and what goes wrong

Minimizing wirelength alone collapses all cells onto one point. So global placement adds a density constraint that spreads cells, legalization snaps them into rows without overlap, and detailed placement polishes locally. A placement that packs cells too tightly in one region creates routing congestion: more wires want to cross a region than there are tracks. A placement that ignores timing makes critical nets long. Both failures surface only in later stages, routing and timing analysis, which is why placers now include congestion and timing estimates in their objective. Placement quality is therefore judged after routing, not by HPWL alone.

## Going deeper

label: Clock tree synthesis
lesson:
# Clock tree synthesis

Every flip-flop needs the clock, and it needs it at nearly the same time as its neighbours. Clock tree synthesis (CTS) builds the buffered network that distributes the clock from its source to thousands or millions of sinks, controlling skew, slew and power. It runs after placement, when sink locations are known, and before routing, which must honour the clock wires it creates.

## Latency and skew

The insertion delay, or latency, of a sink is the time from the clock source to that sink's clock pin. Skew between two sinks is the difference of their latencies; global skew is the maximum minus the minimum over all sinks. If four sinks have latencies 412, 398, 425 and 405 ps, global skew is $425 - 398 = 27$ ps. CTS aims for small skew between flops that talk to each other, controlled slew at every sink, and low power, since the clock net switches every cycle and often consumes a large share of dynamic power.

## Building the buffered tree

A single driver cannot drive a million sinks, so CTS builds a tree of buffers in which each buffer drives a limited number of loads. If each buffer may drive at most $k$ loads, the leaf level needs $\lceil N/k \rceil$ buffers to serve $N$ sinks, the level above needs $\lceil \cdot/k \rceil$ of those, and so on up to one buffer at the root. For $N = 1000$ and $k = 8$: 125, then 16, then 2, then 1, a total of 144 buffers in 4 levels. Real CTS also balances wire lengths, for example with H-tree structures or by clustering sinks geometrically and balancing delay at each merge point.

## Skew and timing

Skew changes timing checks. For a path from launch flop A to capture flop B, if B's clock arrives later than A's by $\delta$, setup slack grows by $\delta$ and hold slack shrinks by $\delta$. Skew is therefore not purely bad: useful-skew optimization delays some clocks on purpose to borrow time for critical paths. But skew that CTS did not intend, from a bad tree or from on-chip variation, can create hold violations that appear only after CTS. That is why the flow re-runs timing analysis and hold fixing immediately after CTS.

## Going deeper

label: Global and detailed routing
lesson:
# Global and detailed routing

Routing turns every net's connectivity into metal wires and vias on the available layers, without breaking design rules and without shorting nets together. It runs in two phases. Global routing assigns each net to a coarse path through a grid of routing regions, managing congestion. Detailed routing then draws exact tracks and vias inside each region. Routing failures are where earlier placement and floorplan decisions come due.

## Global routing and overflow

The global router divides the chip into a grid of rectangular regions called gcells. Each boundary between two adjacent gcells has a capacity: the number of tracks that cross it. Capacity per layer is the boundary length divided by the track pitch, and the layer's preferred direction decides which boundaries it serves. A gcell edge 10 $\mu m$ long with a pitch of 0.2 $\mu m$ has 50 tracks per layer, so three layers in that direction give 150. Each net's path adds one unit of demand to every boundary it crosses. Overflow on an edge is $\max(0, \text{demand} - \text{capacity})$, and the global router rips up and reroutes nets until total overflow is zero or as small as possible.

## Detailed routing and design rules

Detailed routing assigns each net segment to a specific track and layer and inserts vias between layers, obeying spacing, width, via enclosure and many more rules from the process. Modern processes have complex rules (minimum area, end-of-line spacing, multiple-patterning colouring), so detailed routers spend most of their effort on repairing design-rule violations. A design that routes with zero overflow can still fail detailed routing if local pin access is too dense. TritonRoute in OpenROAD is an open-source detailed router. Routing runtime is often dominated by the last few hundred violations, which need repeated local rip-up and reroute.

## Detours and what routing reveals

A routed net is usually longer than its HPWL because it detours around congestion and blockages. If a net with HPWL 120 $\mu m$ routes at 138 $\mu m$, it is 15% longer than the placement estimate, and its delay and coupling grow accordingly. Routing is where real wire geometry first exists, so it is also where crosstalk, antenna effects and actual wire delay appear. A design that met timing with placement estimates can fail after routing, and severe congestion may force a return to placement or even the floorplan.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Extraction, timing and signoff

Signoff is the set of final checks that must all pass before a design is sent to manufacturing. Parasitic extraction computes the resistance and capacitance of every routed wire; static timing analysis uses them to check every path at every corner; power, IR-drop and electromigration analysis check the supply; design-rule and layout-versus-schematic checks verify the geometry. A signoff check is meant to be trusted, so signoff tools favour accuracy over speed.

## Parasitic extraction

Once wires exist, an extractor computes each net's resistance from wire length, width and sheet resistance, and its capacitance to ground and to neighbouring nets from the geometry and the dielectric stack. The result is an RC network per net, written as SPEF. Extraction is pattern-based for speed in most of the design and uses field solvers where accuracy matters. Coupling capacitance is the important new information: it makes a net's delay depend on whether its neighbours switch at the same time, which is crosstalk. Extracted coupling also feeds signal-integrity checks for glitches on quiet nets.

## Corners, modes and scenarios

A chip must work across process variation, supply voltage and temperature (PVT), and with interconnect at its own extremes (RC corners such as worst capacitance or worst RC). It must also work in every functional mode: normal operation, test mode, low-power modes. Signoff timing runs each combination as a scenario. With 3 modes, 4 PVT corners and 3 RC corners, there are $3 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 36$ scenarios. Tools prune dominated scenarios, but large designs still sign off dozens, which is why multi-scenario timing must be fast and incremental.

## Signoff slack with real parasitics

With extracted parasitics, setup slack at a flop is $T - (t_{cq} + t_{logic} + t_{wire}) - t_{setup}$, adjusted for skew and uncertainty. Wire delay estimated before routing is often too low. If a path with a 1000 ps clock had $t_{cq} = 60$, $t_{logic} = 700$, an estimated $t_{wire} = 120$ and $t_{setup} = 40$ ps, its slack was 80 ps. If extraction shows wire delay 50% higher, 180 ps, slack becomes 20 ps. Paths that fail at signoff are fixed with engineering change orders (ECOs): small, local edits such as resizing a gate or inserting a buffer, followed by incremental re-routing and re-extraction.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009); the OpenSTA and OpenRCX documentation.

# Tape-out, fabrication, packaging and test

Tape-out is the moment the design team releases final layout to the foundry. After it, the design leaves the EDA world for the factory: mask making, wafer fabrication, wafer test, dicing, packaging and final test. Months pass between tape-out and working parts in hand, and any bug that reaches this point costs a respin. Knowing what happens after tape-out explains why signoff is so conservative.

## Tape-out and mask data preparation

At tape-out the team delivers GDSII or OASIS layout plus documentation. The foundry and the mask shop then run mask data preparation: fill insertion if not already done, optical proximity correction (OPC), which pre-distorts shapes so that they print correctly through lithography, and fracturing of the polygons into the form a mask writer exposes. One mask is made per lithography layer (and more under multiple patterning), so an advanced process needs a set of dozens of masks, which is a large share of a respin's cost. Mask data preparation is itself a large compute job.

## Fabrication

Wafer fabrication builds the transistors first (front-end-of-line) and then the metal interconnect stack (back-end-of-line) through hundreds of process steps: lithography, etching, deposition, implantation, polishing. Fabrication takes weeks to months. The foundry monitors the process with test structures in the scribe lines between dies. Engineering lots, the first wafers of a new design, may be run faster at higher cost to get silicon for debug sooner. Process variation between wafers and across a wafer is why silicon is tested and binned rather than assumed identical. For the design team, the fabrication wait is when test programs, bring-up boards and software are prepared, so that first silicon can be debugged immediately.

## Packaging and production test

Wafer sort probes every die on the wafer and marks failing ones. Good dies are diced, assembled into packages (wire-bond or flip-chip, possibly with other dies in an advanced package) and tested again in final test, often across temperature. Production test runs the scan patterns and memory built-in self-test that DFT made possible, plus parametric checks and speed binning, in which parts are sorted by the frequency they reach. Test escapes, defective parts that pass test, are counted as defective parts per million shipped. When first silicon fails, engineers debug it with scan diagnosis and physical failure analysis, then decide between a metal-only fix, which changes a few masks, and a full respin.

## Going deeper

Plummer, Deal and Griffin, "Silicon VLSI Technology: Fundamentals, Practice and Modeling" (2000); Bushnell and Agrawal, "Essentials of Electronic Testing".

lesson:
# Why design flows iterate

The flow diagram is a straight line, but no real project runs it once. Timing, power, area and verification are checked at many stages with better information each time, and when a later check fails, an earlier stage re-runs. Design closure is the process of converging that loop. For a tool designer, the shape of the loop sets what matters: fast estimates early, accurate analysis late, and incremental engines everywhere.

## The same question asked many times

Timing is estimated in synthesis with wire-load models or virtual placement, re-estimated after placement with HPWL-based wires, after CTS with real clock skew, after routing with extracted parasitics, and finally signed off across all corners. Power and area follow a similar ladder. Each estimate is cheaper and less accurate than the next. A stage optimizes against the estimate it has, so each estimate's error becomes a later stage's surprise. Closure is fast when early estimates correlate well with signoff, and slow when they do not. Correlation between stages is measured and tracked like any other QoR metric.

## Loops and their costs

When a check fails, the cheapest fix is the most local one. A failing path at signoff is first tried with an ECO: resize, buffer, reroute. If that fails, the block may be re-placed with new constraints. If placement cannot fix it, the floorplan or even the RTL changes. Each step back re-runs every stage after it, so the loops are nested and their costs multiply. Typical loops are the timing-closure loop (placement through signoff), the congestion loop (placement and routing), and the functional loop (RTL and verification), which can reopen everything downstream.

## Convergence and when it fails

Iteration helps only if it converges. Two fixes can fight: upsizing gates for setup adds area and power and can cause hold violations; spreading cells to relieve congestion lengthens critical wires. A flow converges when each loop reduces the violations without creating as many elsewhere. Practical safeguards include margins in early stages (over-constraining the clock in synthesis), correlation work that calibrates fast estimates against signoff, and incremental tools that re-analyze only what changed, so each iteration costs minutes rather than a full run. When none of these works, the team changes a constraint or the architecture instead of iterating forever.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 8 on timing closure.

lesson:
# How poor decisions propagate downstream

A flow is a directed sequence of stages, and an error made in one stage is inherited by every stage after it. Fixing it means changing the stage that made it and re-running all of its descendants. The cost of a decision is therefore not the cost of its own stage but of everything downstream that depends on it. That arithmetic explains ECOs, margins and the value of catching problems early.

## Re-running the descendants

Treat the flow as a chain: synthesis, scan insertion, floorplan, placement, CTS, routing, extraction, signoff. A change at stage $k$ invalidates the outputs of stage $k$ and all stages after it. In a chain of 8 stages, a change at floorplan (stage 3) forces 6 stages to re-run: floorplan, placement, CTS, routing, extraction and signoff. A change at routing forces 3. In a real flow the dependency structure is a DAG rather than a chain, and the set to re-run is everything reachable from the changed node, which a topological order of the DAG gives directly.

## Adding up the cost

If each stage has a run time, the cost of a change is the sum over the stages that must re-run. Suppose floorplan 2 h, placement 6 h, CTS 3 h, routing 10 h, extraction 2 h and signoff 5 h. A floorplan change costs $2 + 6 + 3 + 10 + 2 + 5 = 28$ h of compute before the result is known, while a routing-level ECO costs $10 + 2 + 5 = 17$ h, or less with incremental routing. That gap is why engineers push fixes as late and as locally as they can.

## Iterations that may fail

A re-run does not always succeed. If each attempt closes with probability $q$, independently, the number of attempts is geometric with mean $1/q$. With $q = 0.4$ and 28 h per attempt, the expected time to closure is $28/0.4 = 70$ h. Poor early decisions lower $q$: a floorplan with too little white space makes every placement attempt likelier to fail. The expected cost of a decision is its downstream run time divided by the success probability it leaves, which is why good floorplans and realistic constraints pay off many times.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 1 on the design flow and its iterations.

lesson:
# The map of design representations and formats

A design passes through a dozen representations on its way from RTL to masks, and each one is stored in a file format that tools exchange. Each format keeps some information, drops some, and lets a particular tool compute something it could not compute otherwise. A tool designer reads formats the way a compiler writer reads intermediate representations: as contracts that say what the next stage may assume.

## The main formats and what they keep

RTL in Verilog, SystemVerilog or VHDL keeps cycle-level behaviour and drops gates and geometry. A gate-level netlist (usually structural Verilog) keeps cells and their connections and drops behaviour inside cells and all geometry. Liberty keeps each cell's function, timing and power as tables and drops its transistors. SDC keeps the designer's timing intent: clocks, input and output delays, exceptions. LEF keeps each cell's outline, pin shapes and routing blockages, and the technology's layers and rules, while dropping the cell's internals. DEF keeps a design's placement and routing. SPEF keeps extracted wire resistance and capacitance. GDSII and OASIS keep the final polygons on every mask layer and drop connectivity. A SPICE netlist keeps transistors and passive devices for circuit simulation.

## Who writes and who reads each format

Formats map onto stages. The designer writes RTL and SDC. Library characterization writes Liberty; the library provider writes LEF. Logic synthesis writes the gate netlist, which placement, routing, equivalence checking and gate-level simulation read. Floorplanning, placement and routing write DEF. Extraction writes SPEF, which static timing and power analysis read. Stream-out after routing writes GDSII or OASIS, which physical verification and mask preparation read. Delay calculation can write SDF (standard delay format), which gate-level timing simulation reads. Knowing the producer and consumer of each file tells you where a corrupt file came from and which stage it will break.

## Choosing the format for a computation

Each analysis needs a specific set of formats. Static timing analysis needs the netlist (structure), Liberty (cell delays), SDC (constraints) and, at signoff, SPEF (wire parasitics). Placement needs the netlist, LEF (cell sizes and pins) and the floorplan in DEF. Design-rule checking needs only GDSII or OASIS and the foundry's rule deck, because it is a purely geometric check. Layout-versus-schematic needs the layout and a reference netlist. A request such as "compute coupling-aware delay" therefore implies SPEF with coupling capacitances, not just a netlist. Power analysis similarly needs Liberty power tables plus switching activity from simulation, recorded as VCD or SAIF.

## Going deeper

The Liberty reference manual, the LEF/DEF language reference (distributed through Si2), IEEE 1481 for SPEF, and the OpenROAD documentation on its database (OpenDB).

lesson:
# Netlists as the shared currency of the flow

A netlist is the list of component instances in a design and the nets that connect their pins. It is the representation almost every stage reads or writes: synthesis produces it, placement and routing attach geometry to it, timing and power analyze it, LVS compares against it. Mathematically a netlist is a hypergraph, and the way a tool turns that hypergraph into a graph decides what its algorithms can do.

## Instances, pins and nets

Each instance references a master cell from a library, for example U17 of type NAND2. Each master has pins with directions: inputs, outputs, inouts. A net connects a set of pins: usually one driver (an output pin or a primary input) and one or more sinks. The fanout of a net is its number of sink pins. A netlist file says nothing about where cells are or how they behave inside; the master names point into Liberty and LEF for that. Netlists are usually hierarchical, with module instances inside modules, and tools flatten them on demand.

## The netlist as a hypergraph

Model each instance as a vertex and each net as a hyperedge, the set of instances whose pins it connects. A net with $p$ pins is one hyperedge of size $p$. Counting is the first computation: the total pin count is the sum of hyperedge sizes, and the number of nets is the number of hyperedges. If a netlist has nets with 2, 3, 2, 5 and 4 pins, it has 5 nets and 16 pin connections, and the 5-pin net has a fanout of 4. Partitioners such as hMETIS and the Fiduccia-Mattheyses algorithm work on the hypergraph directly, counting how many hyperedges a cut splits.

## Graph models of a hypergraph

Many algorithms need an ordinary graph. The clique model replaces a $p$-pin net with all $p(p - 1)/2$ pairwise edges, usually weighted by $1/(p - 1)$ or similar so that large nets do not dominate. The star model adds one new vertex per net and $p$ edges to it. A 5-pin net becomes 10 edges as a clique or 5 as a star. Quadratic placers use these models to write wirelength as a quadratic form, and the choice changes both the result and the problem size: a single 1000-pin net becomes almost half a million clique edges, which is why large nets are given star models or ignored in early placement.

lesson:
# Boolean networks, BDDs and AIGs

Before logic becomes cells it lives in a technology-independent representation of Boolean functions. Three dominate: the Boolean network (a DAG of nodes, each with a local function), the binary decision diagram (BDD), a canonical graph for a single function under a variable order, and the and-inverter graph (AIG), a DAG of two-input AND nodes with optionally inverted edges. Synthesis, equivalence checking and formal verification all choose among them, and the choice decides what is cheap.

## Truth tables and their size

The plainest representation of an $n$-input function is its truth table, with $2^n$ rows. It is canonical (two functions are equal exactly when their tables are equal) but exponential, so it is used only for small cuts, typically up to 6 to 16 inputs, inside larger algorithms. The number of distinct $n$-input Boolean functions is $2^{2^n}$: 16 for $n = 2$ and 65,536 for $n = 4$. Technology mappers and rewriting engines in ABC enumerate small cuts and compare their truth tables, which is fast precisely because the cuts are small.

## And-inverter graphs

An AIG represents any function with two-input AND nodes and inverters on edges. An $n$-input AND needs $n - 1$ nodes. An $n$-input OR also needs $n - 1$, by De Morgan's law: $a + b = \overline{\bar a \cdot \bar b}$. A two-input XOR needs 3 nodes, and so does a two-to-one multiplexer. A network built from a 4-input AND, a 3-input OR and one XOR without shared logic has $3 + 2 + 3 = 8$ AND nodes. AIGs are not canonical, but they are compact, uniform and fast to rewrite, which is why ABC and Yosys use them as the working form for logic optimization and why the AIGER format exists to exchange them.

## BDDs and canonicity

A reduced ordered BDD fixes a variable order and merges identical subgraphs, so each function has exactly one BDD for that order. Equivalence becomes pointer comparison. Size depends strongly on the order. An $n$-input AND has $n$ internal nodes; $n$-input parity has $2n - 1$ (one node at the top level, two at each level below). Some functions, such as multipliers, have exponentially large BDDs under every order. So BDDs serve where canonicity pays (small blocks, some model checking, don't-care computation), while SAT on AIGs carries most large equivalence and formal checks.

## Going deeper

Bryant, "Graph-Based Algorithms for Boolean Function Manipulation", IEEE Transactions on Computers (1986); Mishchenko, Chatterjee and Brayton, "DAG-Aware AIG Rewriting" (DAC 2006); the ABC documentation.

lesson:
# Liberty cell libraries

Liberty is the format that tells synthesis, timing and power tools how each library cell behaves. It replaces a cell's transistors with tables: delay and output slew as functions of input slew and output load, power per transition, leakage, pin capacitances, logic function and timing checks for sequential cells. It is the abstraction that makes static timing analysis of a billion-transistor chip possible, and its accuracy limits the accuracy of everything that reads it.

## What a Liberty file contains

A Liberty library declares units (for example time in ns, capacitance in pF), the operating condition it was characterized at (one process, voltage and temperature), and then one cell group per cell. Each cell lists pins with direction and capacitance, a function string such as `!(A & B)` for a NAND2, and timing arcs from each input to each output. Each arc holds lookup tables, the nonlinear delay model (NLDM), indexed by input transition and output load. Sequential cells add setup, hold and clock-to-output arcs. A separate Liberty file exists for each characterized corner.

## Reading and interpolating a table

A timing table is a grid. Suppose a NAND2's rise delay row at a given input slew has loads 0.01, 0.02, 0.04 pF with delays 0.050, 0.068, 0.101 ns. At a load of exactly 0.02 pF the delay is the table value, 0.068 ns. At 0.03 pF the tool interpolates linearly between the neighbouring entries:
$$d = 0.068 + \frac{0.03 - 0.02}{0.04 - 0.02}(0.101 - 0.068) = 0.0845\ \text{ns}.$$
With both slew and load between grid points the tool interpolates bilinearly. Outside the table it extrapolates, which is less accurate and which timers flag.

## Power, leakage and what tables miss

Liberty also holds internal switching energy per arc and leakage power per cell, sometimes per input state. Total leakage of a block is the sum over instances: 4000 cells at 2.5 nW and 1500 at 6 nW leak $10{,}000 + 9{,}000 = 19{,}000$ nW, or 19 $\mu$W. Tables have limits. NLDM models the output as a ramp, which is poor for long resistive wires and very small geometries, so current-source models (CCS, ECSM) store output current waveforms instead. Statistical extensions (the Liberty variation format) add per-arc sigma for on-chip variation. A library missing a corner, or with coarse tables, propagates its error into every timing and power number downstream.

## Going deeper

The Liberty user guide and reference manual (Synopsys, distributed through its open library program); the OpenSTA documentation on Liberty support.

lesson:
# SDC timing constraints

Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) is the Tcl-based format in which designers state timing intent: which clocks exist and at what period, when inputs arrive and outputs are required relative to those clocks, and which paths are exceptions. Synthesis, placement, CTS, routing optimization and static timing analysis all read the same SDC. A wrong constraint is worse than a slow tool: every engine will optimize faithfully toward the wrong target.

## Clocks

The command `create_clock -name clk -period 2.5 [get_ports clk]` declares a clock with a 2.5 ns period, which is $1000/2.5 = 400$ MHz. Generated clocks derived from it, for example a divide-by-two, are declared with `create_generated_clock`. `set_clock_uncertainty` subtracts margin for jitter and expected skew from every check, and `set_clock_latency` describes clock delay before CTS has built the real tree. Clocks with no defined relationship are declared asynchronous so that the timer does not check impossible paths between them. The clock definitions are the root of every timing check, so a wrong period or a missing clock makes every downstream slack meaningless.

## Input and output delays

A block's ports connect to logic outside it, so SDC states how much of the clock period that outside logic uses. `set_input_delay 0.8 -clock clk [get_ports din]` says data reaches the port 0.8 ns after the clock edge. For a register inside the block, the logic from that port must settle by the next edge minus setup and uncertainty. With a 2.5 ns period, a 0.8 ns input delay, a 0.1 ns setup time and 0.15 ns of uncertainty, the internal path has $2.5 - 0.8 - 0.1 - 0.15 = 1.45$ ns. Output delays are the mirror: `set_output_delay` reserves time for logic after the output port.

## Exceptions

Some paths should not be checked with the default single-cycle rule. `set_false_path` removes paths that can never be sensitized or that cross between asynchronous clocks. `set_multicycle_path 2 -setup` lets a path take two cycles, so its setup check moves to the second capture edge: with a 2.5 ns clock, the path has 5 ns minus setup and uncertainty. Exceptions are powerful and dangerous. A false-path constraint written too broadly hides real failures, and nothing in the timer will report it, which is why constraint review and constraint linting are signoff steps.

## Going deeper

Gangadharan and Churiwala, "Constraining Designs for Synthesis and Timing Analysis: A Practical Guide to Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC)" (2013).

lesson:
# LEF and DEF physical exchange

LEF (Library Exchange Format) and DEF (Design Exchange Format) are the text formats in which physical-design tools exchange abstract layout. LEF describes the technology and the library: routing layers, pitches, vias and design rules, plus each cell's outline, pins and obstructions. DEF describes one design: die area, rows, placed components, pins, and routed nets. Placement and routing engines, including OpenROAD, read and write them.

## LEF: abstracts of cells and layers

A technology LEF lists each routing layer with its preferred direction, track pitch, minimum width and spacing, plus via definitions. A cell LEF describes each macro by its class (core cell, block, pad), its size, the site it occupies, its pin shapes on specific layers, and obstructions (OBS) where a router must not draw. It deliberately omits the cell's internal transistors and most internal wiring. That abstraction is exactly what a placer and router need: where a cell may sit, how big it is, and where its pins can be reached.

## DEF: a design in database units

DEF stores coordinates as integers in database units, declared by a line such as `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 1000`, meaning 1000 units per micron. A `DIEAREA ( 0 0 ) ( 1500000 1200000 )` is therefore a 1500 by 1200 micron die, an area of $1.8\ mm^2$. Each component appears with its master and location, for example `- u42 NAND2_X1 + PLACED ( 84000 212800 ) N`, which is at $(84, 212.8)\ \mu m$ with north orientation. Rows are declared with their site and repeat count, and nets carry routed segments once routing is done.

## Rows, sites and capacity

Standard cells sit on a site grid. If the core is 1360 $\mu m$ tall and the site height is 2.72 $\mu m$, the core holds $1360 / 2.72 = 500$ rows. If each row is 1200 $\mu m$ wide with a site width of 0.19 $\mu m$, a row has $\lfloor 1200 / 0.19 \rfloor = 6315$ sites. A cell's width in LEF is a whole number of sites. These counts bound placement capacity, and they show why LEF and DEF must agree: a DEF written with a different site or unit declaration than the LEF it is read with silently misplaces every cell.

The LEF/DEF Language Reference (Cadence, distributed through Si2); the OpenDB documentation in OpenROAD.
